units.title: Soil and Water Conservation
units.intro: Land degradation here is mostly **water erosion** on slopes after cover is removed, plus wind on bare dry plains, salinity where irrigation is careless, and fertility mining.

f2.title: Same idea as Geography Unit 5: hold the rain where it falls.

cards.title: 3.1.1 Definition of Soil and Water Conservation
body: Soil and water conservation refers to practices which involve all human activities aimed at reducing the removal of the soil from the land, as well as protecting and maintaining the water supply.

cards.title: 3.1.2 The Importance of Soil and Water Conservation
body: Soil and water conservation has long history in Eritrea.

Farming has been carried out for thousands of years, and traditional soil and water conservation methods have evolved at the local level in response to the evolution of the agricultural system in Eritrea.
Eritrea is located in the Sudano-Sahelian region of Africa, where rainfall is not only low but also erratic, with great variations between years.
Precipitation is unevenly distributed geographically, with large parts of the country being too dry for rain-fed agriculture.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: What percentage of topsoil and organic matter is primarily lost during sheet erosion?

steps.text: **Reasoning**
Sheet erosion involves the removal of a thin, uniform layer of topsoil over a wide area.
Because organic matter and key nutrients are concentrated in the topsoil (the uppermost layer), sheet erosion selectively strips away this most fertile portion of the soil.
**Conclusion**
Therefore, the correct answer is **The most fertile upper layer.**

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: In the standard classification of water erosion, which of the following represents temporary channels that can be easily removed by normal tillage?

steps.text: **Reasoning**
Rills are small, shallow, concentrated runoff paths.
According to soil science definitions, rill channels are temporary and can be easily smoothed out and obliterated by normal agricultural tillage operations (such as plowing).
**Conclusion**
Thus, the temporary channels are **Rill channels**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the primary agent responsible for the physical soil degradation known as wind deflation in dry plains?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Deflation is the process by which wind lifts and removes loose, fine-grained, dry particles from the soil surface. This occurs primarily in arid and semi-arid climates where wind velocities are high and vegetation cover is scanty.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, the primary agent is **High-velocity wind**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: According to standard definitions, soil salinization in irrigated fields is primarily caused by which of the following?

options.A: The loss of nitrogenous organic matter.
options.B: The accumulation of excess soluble salts in the root zone.
options.C: The physical compaction of topsoil by machinery.
options.D: The direct impact of high-velocity raindrops.
options.E: An excessive rate of cover crop nitrogen fixation.

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Salinization is the accumulation of water-soluble salts in the soil profile, particularly in the root zone of crops. It commonly becomes a problem in arid areas under irrigation when poor-quality, saline water is applied without adequate drainage.

**Conclusion**
Thus, salinization is **the accumulation of excess soluble salts in the root zone**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What percentage of topsoil and organic matter is primarily lost during sheet erosion?

options.E: The entire soil profile down to bedrock.

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Sheet erosion involves the removal of a thin, uniform layer of topsoil over a wide area. Because organic matter and key nutrients are concentrated in the topsoil (the uppermost layer), sheet erosion selectively strips away this most fertile portion of the soil.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, the correct answer is **The most fertile upper layer.**

cards.title: 3.2.1 Types of Land Degradation
body: Land degradation is a process that lowers the current and/ or potential capability of land to produce goods and services.
Continued deterioration of land leads to a permanent decrease in its biological potential and deterioration of living conditions for the inhabitants.
Land degradation is both a process and a phenomenon.

As a process, land degradation is continuous and incremental, and marked by increased weakening of the physical, biological and economic potential of the land through a drastic reduction in overall productivity.

cards.title: 3.2.2 Causes and Effects of Land Degradation
body: The main causes for land degradation are complex and attributed to a combination of biophysical, social, economic and political factors.
One such view considers population pressure to be the main cause of deforestation, overgrazing and expansion of cultivation into marginal lands.
High population density is not necessarily related to land degradation; it is what a population does to the land that determines the extent of degradation.
People can be a major asset in reversing a trend towards degradation.

cards.title: 3.2.3 Soil Erosion
body: Erosion is a gravity driven process that transports solids in the natural environment and deposits them elsewhere.
Erosion is a natural process, but its magnitude has increased dramatically due to human land-use practices, especially industrial agriculture, deforestation and urban sprawl.
Land that is used for industrial agriculture generally experiences a significantly faster rate of erosion than land under natural vegetation, or land used for sustainable agricultural practices.
Tillage reduces vegetation cover on the surface of the soil and disturbs both soil structure and plant roots that would otherwise hold the soil in place.

**Conclusion**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is classified as a physical (mechanical) soil and water conservation measure?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Physical measures involve engineering earthworks or constructing physical barriers. Constructing check dams across gullies is a mechanical engineering structure. All other options are biological or agronomic measures.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, the physical measure is **Check Dam construction**.

cards.title: 3.3.1 Surveying/Contouring
body: Vertical interval (VI) is the difference in height (elevation) between two points on a slope.
Slope steepness can be expressed in four different ways: • Angle in degrees: This is the angle that the slope makes with the horizontal.
Metres per metre: This is vertical interval divided by horizontal.
For example a canal gradient of 0.4 per cent can be shown as 0.004 m/m.

cards.title: 3.3.2 Physical SWC Measures
body: Physical SWC measures usually comprise engineering works involving the construction of earthworks such as terraces, earth dams and water diversions.
The earthworks intercept and slow runoff water, which then prevent sheet, rill and gully erosion.
The intercepted water soaks into the soil.
Hillside terraces: A hillside terrace is hillside ditch or ridge for controlling the flow of surface water down a slope.

cards.title: 3.3.3 Biological SWC Measures
body: Vegetative SWC measures can be used in various land uses.
Vegetative conservation measures can be used on uncultivated hillsides, to conserve cultivated lands and for the protection of riverbanks.

cards.title: 3.3.4 Agronomic Practices
body: Agronomic practices are those cultural or biological practices for management of annual and perennial crops that promote SWC.
Soil management can be defined as the sum total of all tillage operations, cropping practices, fertilizer, lime and other treatments conducted on, or applied to, a soil for the production of plants.

Water management is the techniques and practices through which available water (rainwater, floodwater, plant available water in soils) is conserved and used with minimum wastage for sustainable agricultural production.
Soil and water management include all farming practices applied on land, through which soils and water are conserved and used with minimum wastage for sustained agricultural production.

cards.title: 3.4.1 Dams
body: Dams and reservoirs are designed to stem the flow of water and store as much of it as possible.
Surface water is stored either in natural lakes and wetlands or in artificial storage structures created by the construction of dams.
Dams are constructed for the purpose of water storage for irrigation, hydro-electric power generation, flood control or any combination of these.

cards.title: 3.4.2 Ponds
body: Ponds are bodies of water created by excavating a pit or by constructing a short embankment across a water source.
Ponds are used to store small supplies of water.
In Eritrea, all ponds are small, with a capacity of 500–5000 m3 of water, and are used for short periods of time.
The number of ponds is increasing, especially in places where the climate is arid.

cards.title: 3.4.3 River Diversion
body: A diversion structure is a structure built across a river to divert regulated quantities of water towards a canal.
Figures 3.16 shows two examples of a diversion structure built across rivers in Sheeb and Gash-Barka.
Establish the major purposes of diversion structures.

cards.title: 3.4.4 Wells
body: Most parts of Eritrea receive very little rainfall.
Wells are commonly used for drawing water from sub-surface dams.
A well should be located on the upper side of a stream, close to the dam embankment.
Wells are usually constructed close to or in riverbeds, valleys and flat areas.

cards.title: 3.4.5 Roof and Rock Outcrop Water-Harvesting
body: How do they do this Roof water-harvesting is one of the most important waterharvesting techniques in dry areas.
Houses constructed with concrete roofs or corrugated iron sheets are excellent for collecting water.
The water from the roof is collected and channelled into concrete cisterns for household use.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is the most water-efficient irrigation method, delivering water drop-by-drop near the root zone?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Drip (or trickle) irrigation is the most water-efficient irrigation method ($$90\% - 95\%$$\text{ efficiency}) because it delivers water directly to the root zone of the plant, drop-by-drop, minimizing evaporation and deep percolation.

**Conclusion**
Thus, the most efficient method is **Drip irrigation**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Why is proper soil drainage essential for fruit tree production?

options.A: It prevents the leaves from absorbing too much nitrogen.
options.B: Fruit tree roots suffocate and can die if waterlogged for even a week.
options.C: It increases the atmospheric wind speed around the orchard.
options.D: It prevents the soil from compacting under the weight of the fruit.
options.E: It eliminates the need for any subsequent organic manuring.

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Fruit trees are highly sensitive to waterlogging. Even on excellent soils, just one week of waterlogging is enough to suffocate and kill fruit tree roots, causing a severe loss of productivity.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, drainage is essential because **roots suffocate and die if waterlogged for even a week**.

cards.why: Dams are large-scale structures built across rivers or valleys to store vast amounts of water for irrigation, electricity, or human consumption. Ponds are much smaller.

cards.title: Irrigation and drainage
body: Water conservation = store (ponds, dams), sink (infiltration), save (mulch, drip where possible), don’t waste or pollute.

cards.title: 3.5.1 Irrigation
body: Irrigation is the process by which water is conveyed from the source to the crop through open or closed canals or pipes.

Archaeological investigation has identified evidence of irrigation in Mesopotamia, Egypt and Iran which were built as far back as the 6th millennium BCE, where barley was grown in areas where the natural rainfall was insufficient to support such a crop.
In many parts of the world, there is a deficiency of soil water for crop production for part or all the year, and staple crop production depends on irrigation.
The use of ground water for irrigation enables the extension of the irrigated area.

cards.title: 3.5.2 The Importance of Irrigation
body: Agriculture is often cited as the principal “user” of raw water.
In arid and semi-arid areas, irrigation is used to extend cultivation, to increase yield and to insure against high rainfall variability.
In humid areas, supplementary irrigation is used to overcome the soil water deficit that may occur at a critical period of the cropgrowing season.
Water infiltrates into the soil, evaporates or runs off as surface water.

cards.title: 3.5.3 Methods of Irrigation
body: Various types of irrigation technique differ on how the water obtained from the source is distributed within the field.
In general, the object of irrigation is to supply the entire field uniformly with water so that each plant has the amount of water it needs – neither too much nor too little.
Surface irrigation is usually relatively cheaper to install but more expensive to operate.
Modern irrigation systems are relatively expensive, and offer lower operating costs and higher water-use efficiency.

cards.title: 3.5.4 Drainage
body: Drainage is a practice of removing excess water from the soil surface and upper layer of the sub-soil, in order to improve the soil conditions for growing crops.
Poorly drained soils are not well aerated due to saturation with water.
Soil fertility in poorly drained soils is very low, giving rise to patchy plants with stunted roots and reduced growth.

cards.title: 3.5.5 The Importance of Drainage
body: In moist climates, soils may be adequate for cropping, with the exception of when they become waterlogged for brief periods each year from snow melt or heavy rains.
Soils that are predominantly clay filter water very slowly downward, meanwhile, plant roots suffocate because the excessive water around the roots eliminates aeration in the soil.
Other soils may have an impervious layer of mineralized soil, called a hardpan, or a relatively impervious rock layer may underlie shallow soils.
Excellent soils may be waterlogged for one week of the year, which is sufficient enough to kill fruit trees, causing a loss of land productivity until replacements can be established.

cards.title: 3.5.6 Types of Drainage Systems
body: Shallow ditches, also called open drains, normally accomplish surface drainage.
The shallow ditches discharge into larger and deeper collection drains.
In order to facilitate the flow of excess water toward the drains, the field is given an artificial slope by means of land grading.
When compared to surface and sub-surface drainage systems, this method works well in poorly permeable topsoil overlying rapidly permeable and deep sub-soil.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which type of drainage system uses trees with high water requirements, such as Eucalyptus species, to naturally transpire excess water?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Bio-drainage is a biological drainage method where deep-rooted vegetation with high transpiration rates (such as *Eucalyptus* species) is planted to draw up and remove excess water from waterlogged soils.

**Conclusion**
This biological system is **Bio-drainage**.

glossary.meaning: Land degradation is a process that lowers the current and/ or potential capability of land to produce goods and services.
Water erosion is the most widespread form of erosion, while wind erosion is particularly severe in the arid and semi-arid areas.
Erosion is a gravity driven process that transports solids in the natural environment and deposits them elsewhere.
Soil erosion is a serious environmental problem that prevails throughout the whole of Eritrea.
Splash erosion is the detachment and airborne movement of small soil particles caused by the impact of raindrops on soil.
Sheet erosion is the detachment of soil particles by raindrop impact and their removal down slope by water flowing overland as a sheet instead of in definite channels or rills.
Irrigation is the artificial application of water to the soil.
Drainage is a practice of removing excess water from the soil surface and upper layer of the sub-soil, in order to improve the soil conditions for growing crops.
Salinity is the accumulation of excess salts, which are harmful to crops and should be removed.

tips.text: Soil and water conservation refers to practices involving all the human activities aimed at reducing the loss of soil from the land, as well as protecting and maintaining the water supply.
It concerns practical farming measures taken in order to protect land from damage and prevent water wastage.
The speed and extent of soil degradation depends on different factors, such as types of soils, relief, climate and the intensity of land use.
Loss of land-resource productivity is an important problem in Eritrea and, coupled with a growing population, is likely to become critical in the future.
Diverse areas are affected differently by soil degradation.
The Highlands of Eritrea are the areas of greatest livestock density and where major land degradation occurs.
Land degradation is a process that lowers the current and/ or potential capability of land to produce goods and services.
Continued deterioration of land leads to a permanent decrease in its biological potential and deterioration of living conditions for the inhabitants.
Land degradation is both a process and a phenomenon.

As a phenomenon, it is the consequence of a long period marked by diminishing arable land per peasant household, declining land productivity, decreasing livestock production, loss of vegetation cover, shortages of fuel wood and wood materials, loss of topsoil and generalized ecological imbalances.
Biological: Cover crops, grass strips, afforestation, enclosures, controlled grazing.
Mechanical: Contour ploughing, terraces and bunds, check dams, cut-off drains, sub-surface dams in sandy wadis.

questions.q: The main erosion on Eritrean highland slopes is usually

options.C: Running water after cover is lost

why: Answer C: Running water after cover is lost
On the steep highland slopes, once vegetation is removed, heavy rain runs off as sheet flow and forms rills and gullies — water erosion is the main type.

similar.q: Contour bunds are built  A) Straight down the steepest line  B) Across the slope, level with the contour  C) Only in the sea  D) Inside the rumen
similar.a: B. Across the slope, level with the contour

questions.q: Contour bunds are built

options.B: Across the slope, level with the contour

why: Answer B: Across the slope, level with the contour
A contour bund follows the contour (a line of equal height) across the slope, so water is held along it and soaks in instead of running downhill and carrying soil.

questions.q: While inspecting a gently sloping cropland near Keren, a farmer finds many small, shallow, parallel channels running down the field, each only about 20 cm deep. Which type of water erosion is this, and why can the farmer still correct it with ordinary tillage?

options.A: Splash erosion, because raindrop impact has formed a hard surface crust
options.B: Sheet erosion, because the channels are broad, thin sheets of flowing water
options.C: Rill erosion, because these are small, shallow, concentrated flow channels that ordinary farm tillage can smooth out
options.D: Gully erosion, because the channels are narrow and deep and cannot be destroyed by normal tillage

why: **Recall the classification of water erosion.** The unit divides water erosion into four types: splash (raindrop) erosion, sheet erosion, rill erosion and gully erosion.

**Match the field evidence to a type.** The field shows small, shallow, concentrated flow paths (channels) rather than craters from raindrop impact or a uniform thin sheet of moving water. Small, shallow, concentrated flow paths are the defining feature of rill erosion.

**Check the depth against the unit data.** The unit records rill channels as up to $$30\text{ cm}$$ deep, so the measured 20 cm depth falls inside the rill range, while gullies are $$1 - 150\text{ meters}$$ deep.
**Decide on correctability.** The unit states that rills are temporary and can easily be smoothed out by ordinary farm tillage operations, unlike gullies, which cannot be destroyed by normal tillage.

**Evaluate the distractors.** A is wrong because splash erosion creates small craters and a hard crust, not channels. B is wrong because sheet erosion removes soil uniformly in broad, thin sheets, not in defined small channels. D is wrong because the channels are shallow and the unit reserves the non-tillable, deep category for gullies.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: On a bare, sloping plot at Tsorona, raindrops strike the unprotected soil and small crater-like marks appear, with loose soil particles splashed onto the leaves of young maize. The soil surface later dries into a hard crust. Which type of water erosion is responsible?
why: **Recall the four types of water erosion.** Water erosion occurs as splash, sheet, rill and gully erosion, distinguished by how the soil is detached and moved.
**Identify the detachment mechanism.** Here the soil is detached by the direct impact of raindrops on bare soil, which is the definition of splash (raindrop) erosion.

**Confirm with the unit description.** The unit describes splash erosion as producing small craters on bare soil, splashing soil onto plant leaves, destroying soil structure and forming a hard crust on dry soil - all features observed on the plot.
**Rule out the other types.** There is no uniform removal of soil down the slope in thin sheets (sheet), no concentrated channels (rill) and no deep, incised channel (gully).

questions.answer: Gully erosion; it is an advanced stage in which runoff cuts deep channels that cannot be destroyed by normal tillage operations and that divide land into fragments, stopping machinery movement
why: **Match the description to the erosion types.** The feature is a narrow, deep channel formed by surface runoff during or immediately after heavy rains, which is the definition of gully erosion.

questions.q:
Complete the following statements using the correct water-erosion terms.
(1) ................ erosion detaches soil particles by the direct impact of raindrops on bare soil, destroying soil structure and forming a hard crust on dry soil.
(2) ................ erosion develops small, shallow, concentrated flow paths that are temporary and can be easily smoothed out by ordinary farm tillage.
(3) ................ erosion is the advanced stage in which runoff flows in narrow, deep channels that divide land into fragments and cannot be destroyed by normal tillage.
questions.answer: (1) Splash (raindrop) erosion; (2) Rill erosion; (3) Gully erosion
why: **Use the detachment agent to name blank (1).** Blank (1) describes detachment and airborne movement of small soil particles caused by direct raindrop impact on bare soil. The unit calls this splash (raindrop) erosion, and it notes the resulting hard crust on dry soil.

**Use channel size to name blank (2).** Blank (2) describes small, shallow, concentrated flow paths that are temporary and removable by ordinary tillage. This matches rill erosion, with channels up to $$30\text{ cm}$$ deep.

**Use depth and permanence to name blank (3).** Blank (3) describes narrow, deep channels formed during or immediately after heavy rains that divide land into fragments and resist normal tillage. This is gully erosion, ranging from $$1 - 2\text{ meters}$$ to over $$75\text{ meters}$$ deep.
**Check the sequence.** The three blanks follow the unit's progressive order of water erosion: splash then rill then gully, each stage leaving features that are harder to repair than the one before.

**Match the wearing process to blank (2).** The wearing away of plants, rocks and structures by suspended particles in high-velocity winds is abrasion, which also causes sand abrasion on seedlings.

Complete the following statements.
(1) ................ erosion removes soil particles uniformly down a slope in broad, thin sheets rather than in defined channels.
(2) ................ is the imaginary line joining points of the same elevation on the ground surface.

**Identify the surveying term.** The unit defines a contour as an imaginary line joining points of the same elevation on the ground surface, the line along which conservation structures such as contour bunds are laid out.

**Distinguish the two concepts.** Blank (1) names an erosion process that strips the most fertile topsoil and organic matter, while blank (2) names a surveying reference line used to place conservation measures, not an erosion type.

questions.q: A forester uses a line level to check the slope of a gently sloping cropland near Keren before laying out contour bunds. The two identical sticks are set $$10\text{ meters}$$ apart, and the reading on the stick at the lower ground position is $$0.9\text{ meters}$$ greater than the reading on the stick at the higher ground position. Calculate the percentage slope of the plot and state, with justification, whether the site is suitable for contour bunds.
questions.answer: Percentage slope = $$9\%$$; this is slightly steeper than the $$2\% - 8\%$$ ideal range for contour bunds, so bund spacing must be tightened or a stronger physical measure such as hillside terracing used.
why: **Identify what the line level measures.** The unit describes the line level as two identical $$1.5\text{-meter}$$ sticks connected by a $$10\text{-meter}$$ cotton string with a small spirit level suspended in the middle. Because the string is exactly $$10\text{ meters}$$ long, the horizontal interval (HI) is the fixed stick spacing of $$10\text{ meters}$$.

**Obtain the vertical interval.** The vertical interval (VI) is the difference in elevation between the two points. Since both sticks stand vertically, the difference in reading on the sticks equals the difference in ground elevation: $$\text{VI} = 0.9\text{ meters}$$.
**Name the percentage slope formula.** The unit gives $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{\text{VI}}{\text{HI}}\right) \times 100$$.
**Substitute the measured values.** $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{0.9}{10}\right) \times 100 = 0.09 \times 100 = 9\%$$.

**Compare the slope with the ideal site for contour bunds.** The unit table states that contour bunds intercept surface runoff and encourage infiltration on gently sloping croplands of $$2\% - 8\%$$ slope. The computed slope of $$9\%$$ is slightly steeper than that ideal range.

**Conclude with a justified recommendation.** The plot is at $$9\%$$ slope, just above the $$2\% - 8\%$$ band for which contour bunds are the recommended physical measure. Contour bunds would need closer spacing and careful design, and on such a slope a stronger structural measure such as hillside terraces, which break slope length and trap water and sediment on sloping cultivated hills, should be considered.

Compute the percentage slope of the field and decide whether it falls within the slope range for which the unit recommends contour bunds.
questions.answer: Percentage slope = $$4\%$$; this lies within the $$2\% - 8\%$$ range, so contour bunds are suitable
why: **Fix the horizontal interval.** The line level uses a $$10\text{-meter}$$ string, so the sticks are $$10\text{ meters}$$ apart and $$\text{HI} = 10\text{ meters}$$.
**Read off the vertical interval.** The difference in stick readings equals the difference in ground elevation, so $$\text{VI} = 0.4\text{ meters}$$.
**State the formula.** $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{\text{VI}}{\text{HI}}\right) \times 100$$.
**Substitute and compute.** $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{0.4}{10}\right) \times 100 = 0.04 \times 100 = 4\%$$.
**Judge suitability.** $$4\%$$ falls inside the $$2\% - 8\%$$ gently sloping cropland range given for contour bunds, so the site is suitable for this physical measure.

questions.q: On a hillside above Asmara, two points on the ground lie $$50\text{ meters}$$ apart horizontally, and a telescopic level shows that the upper point is $$7.5\text{ meters}$$ higher than the lower point. Compute the percentage slope of this hillside and explain what such a slope means for the choice between contour bunds and hillside terraces.
questions.answer: Percentage slope = $$15\%$$; this far exceeds the $$2\% - 8\%$$ range for contour bunds, so hillside terraces (which break slope length and trap water and sediment) are the appropriate physical measure
why: **Identify the given intervals.** The horizontal distance between the two points is $$\text{HI} = 50\text{ meters}$$ and the elevation difference is $$\text{VI} = 7.5\text{ meters}$$.
**Apply the percentage slope formula.** $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{\text{VI}}{\text{HI}}\right) \times 100$$.
**Substitute and compute.** $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{7.5}{50}\right) \times 100 = 0.15 \times 100 = 15\%$$.

**Interpret the result on the landscape.** A $$15\%$$ slope is nearly twice the upper limit of the $$2\% - 8\%$$ band listed for contour bunds, so bunds alone would not safely handle the runoff on this hillside.

**Select the matching measure.** The unit lists hillside terraces as the physical measure for sloping, cultivated or uncultivated hills because they break slope length, trap water and sediment, and create flat planting steps - the correct choice for a $$15\%$$ hillside.

questions.q: Describe the transition of water erosion from splash erosion to the formation of a highly advanced gully system on a bare, sloping farm plot in the highlands. In your answer, name each stage in order, state the characteristic feature and approximate depth or scale of each, and explain how the farmer could detect the earliest stage of uniform soil removal before channels appear.
questions.answer: The sequence is splash (raindrop) erosion (micro-scale craters, hard crust, particles splashed up to $$1.5\text{ m}$$) then sheet erosion (uniform removal in broad, thin sheets, detectable early by soil pedestals) then rill erosion (small, shallow concentrated channels up to $$30\text{ cm}$$ deep, removable by ordinary tillage) then gully erosion (narrow, deep channels of $$1 - 150\text{ m}$$ that fragment the land and cannot be destroyed by normal tillage).
why: **Start with detachment by raindrop impact.** The process begins with splash (raindrop) erosion, the detachment and airborne movement of small soil particles caused by direct raindrop impact on bare soil. On a micro-scale it produces small craters, destroys soil structure and forms a hard crust on dry soil; the unit notes raindrops can strike bare soil at speeds up to $$30\text{ kilometers per hour}$$ and splash particles up to $$1.5\text{ meters}$$ horizontally.

**Move to uniform removal as sheet erosion.** Once detached, particles are removed uniformly down the slope by water flowing overland in broad, thin sheets rather than in defined channels. Sheet erosion strips very thin layers, removing the most fertile topsoil and organic matter and exposing stone bases.

**Explain how to detect the sheet stage early.** The unit pro-tip advises looking for soil pedestals - tiny columns of soil capped by small stones or wood chips that have protected the soil directly underneath from raindrop impact. Their appearance signals that the surrounding soil is being stripped away in thin sheets before any channels form.

**Describe the appearance of concentrated flow paths.** As overland flow concentrates, rill erosion develops small, shallow, concentrated flow paths that appear as many small, parallel channels across the field, up to $$30\text{ cm}$$ deep. Rills are temporary and can be easily smoothed out by ordinary tillage, so the unit pro-tip warns that if left untreated for even one rainy season they merge and deepen.

**Explain the final, advanced stage.** In the advanced stage the runoff flows in narrow, deep channels during or immediately after heavy rains, producing gullies. Gullies range from $$1\text{ to }2\text{ meters}$$ to over $$75\text{ meters}$$ deep (the unit table gives $$1 - 150\text{ meters}$$), with wide, steep, unstable walls that cannot be destroyed by normal tillage operations.

**State the consequence and the conclusion.** The gully divides the land into fragments and stops machinery movement, making reclamation extremely difficult and expensive. The correct conclusion is that the stages form a continuous, accelerating chain - splash to sheet to rill to gully - so intervention at the rill stage (or earlier, by spotting soil pedestals and applying biological or physical conservation measures) is far cheaper than reclaiming a mature gully.

questions.q: Explain how wind erosion acts on a dry, bare lowland plain such as the eastern dry lowlands, naming its two main effects and describing the damage each does to soil and crops.
questions.answer: Wind erosion acts through deflation, the lifting and removal of loose, light soil particles to another region, and abrasion, the wearing away of plants, rocks and structures by suspended soil particles carried in high-velocity winds; together they strip topsoil and damage seedlings.
why: **State where wind erosion occurs.** The unit states that wind erosion occurs primarily in arid and semi-arid climates where the soil is dry and unprotected by vegetation, which describes the dry lowlands receiving only about $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$ of soil loss by wind.
**Define the first effect.** Deflation is the lifting and removal of loose, light soil particles to another region. It is the primary cause of topsoil blowing away from dry lowland fields.

**Define the second effect.** Abrasion is the wearing away of plants, rocks and structures by suspended soil particles carried in high-velocity winds, and the unit table records it as sand abrasion on seedlings.

**Conclude on the agricultural impact.** Because the dry lowlands have only wind - not rainfall runoff - as the primary causative agent, the conservation response must protect the surface, for example by maintaining vegetative cover and mulch rather than by constructing water-intercepting structures.

questions.q: Explain how rainfall and topography combine to make the Eritrean highlands the most erosion-prone area in the unit's comparison of regions, and state the specific consequences this has for crop production there.
questions.answer: In the highlands, high and intense rainfall produces large volumes of runoff that steep topography accelerates downslope, giving an estimated soil loss of $$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, the highest of the four regions; the consequences are exposed plant roots, severe yield reduction and loss of topsoil.
why: **Recall the two controlling factors.** The unit states that the speed and extent of soil degradation depend on factors such as soil types, topography, climate and the intensity of land use - here climate (rainfall) and topography (slope) are decisive.

**Explain the role of the rainfall factor.** Rainfall in these highland areas supplies the water that detaches particles by raindrop impact and then carries them downslope as runoff, so water is listed as the primary causative agent for the highlands.

**Explain the role of the topographic factor.** Slope steepness increases the velocity of runoff, so the water has more energy to detach and transport soil. The unit records measured soil loss on steep slopes of $$3.4\text{ to }84.5\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$, with a mean of $$42\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$ - about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil annually and roughly $$20\text{ times}$$ the soil replacement rate.

**Apply the regional comparison.** In the unit's table the highlands have the highest estimated loss at $$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, well above the moist lowlands ($$47$$), the eastern escarpment ($$37$$) and the dry lowlands ($$6$$), confirming the highlands as the most erosion-prone region.

**State the agricultural consequences.** The table lists exposed plant roots, severe yield reduction and loss of topsoil for the highlands. The unit adds that erosion depletes nitrogen and phosphorus, lowers water retention capacity, reduces soil depth and exposes roots, making crops highly vulnerable to drought.

questions.q:
A soil conservation team compares two Eritrean sites using the unit's regional soil-loss figures. Site A is highland farmland whose measured loss falls at the lower end of the highland range given in the unit ($$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$). Site B is dry lowland farmland losing $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.
(a) Calculate how many times greater the soil loss at Site A is than at Site B.
(b) The unit also notes that under natural conditions $$1\text{ centimeter}$$ of fertile topsoil takes $$100\text{ to }400\text{ years}$$ to form, and that a loss of about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil per year represents approximately $$20\text{ times}$$ the possible soil replacement rate. Using the mid-point of the formation range ($$250\text{ years}$$ per centimeter), calculate the average annual topsoil formation in millimetres per year, and hence explain in one sentence how Site A's loss compares with it.
questions.answer: (a) Site A ($$50\text{ tons/ha/year}$$) loses about $$8.3\text{ times}$$ as much soil as Site B ($$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$). (b) Using the mid-point of $$250\text{ years}$$ per centimeter, natural topsoil formation averages $$0.04\text{ mm per year}$$, so Site A's loss of roughly $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil per year is about $$100\text{ times}$$ faster than the soil can be replaced.
why: **Extract the soil-loss figures for the two sites.** The unit table gives the highlands an estimated soil loss of $$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$ and the dry lowlands $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$. Site A lies at the lower end of the highland range, so its loss is $$50\text{ tons/ha/year}$$; Site B loses $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.
**State the ratio to be computed.** The required comparison is a ratio: $$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{\text{Loss at Site A}}{\text{Loss at Site B}}$$.
**Substitute and carry out the division.** $$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{50}{6} = 8.33$$, i.e. approximately $$8.3\text{ times}$$.

**Convert the natural formation range into an annual rate.** Under natural conditions $$1\text{ centimeter}$$ ($$= 10\text{ mm}$$) of topsoil needs $$100\text{ to }400\text{ years}$$. Taking the mid-point of $$250\text{ years}$$ per centimeter, the average annual formation is $$\dfrac{10\text{ mm}}{250\text{ years}} = 0.04\text{ mm per year}$$.

**Relate the computed loss rate to the formation rate.** The unit states that a loss of approximately $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil per year is about $$20\text{ times}$$ the possible soil replacement rate. This is consistent with the computed formation rate: $$\dfrac{4\text{ mm}}{0.04\text{ mm per year}} = 100$$ - that is, at the lower-end highland loss of $$50\text{ t/ha/year}$$ the soil is still being removed many times faster than the $$0.04\text{ mm per year}$$ at which fertile topsoil forms naturally.

**State the agronomic consequence.** Because accumulation cannot keep pace with removal, the topsoil layer thins progressively. This matches the unit's description of land degradation as a continuous process marked by progressive weakening of the physical, chemical and biological potential of land, and of erosion causing nutrient depletion (especially nitrogen and phosphorus), lower water retention, reduced soil depth and exposed plant roots.

**Draw the conservation conclusion.** The comparison shows that Site A loses roughly $$8.3\text{ times}$$ as much soil as Site B, and still loses topsoil dozens of times faster than nature rebuilds it, so a physical or biological soil and water conservation measure - for example hillside terraces on the sloping highland plot - is required rather than relying on natural soil formation.

questions.q:
Two farms are compared using the unit's regional figures. Farm X lies in the highlands, where the measured soil loss is at the upper end of the unit's highland range ($$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$). Farm Y lies in the dry lowlands, where the primary causative agent is wind and the estimated loss is $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.
(a) Calculate the ratio of Farm X's soil loss to Farm Y's.
(b) Using the unit figure of about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil lost per year at the mean steep-slope loss rate, and a natural formation time of $$100\text{ years}$$ for $$1\text{ centimeter}$$ of topsoil, calculate the annual natural formation rate and state how many times larger the loss rate is.
questions.answer: (a) $$\dfrac{100}{6} = 16.7$$, so about $$16.7\text{ times}$$ (roughly $$17\text{ times}$$). (b) $$\dfrac{10\text{ mm}}{100\text{ years}} = 0.1\text{ mm per year}$$, so the $$4\text{ mm per year}$$ loss is $$40\text{ times}$$ the natural formation rate
why: **Read the required values from the unit.** The upper end of the highland range is $$100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, so Farm X loses $$100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$; the dry lowland figure is $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, so Farm Y loses $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.
**Compute the ratio.** $$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{100}{6} = 16.7$$, so Farm X loses about $$16.7\text{ times}$$ as much soil as Farm Y.
**Convert formation time to an annual rate.** $$1\text{ centimeter} = 10\text{ mm}$$ forms in $$100\text{ years}$$, so the natural formation rate is $$\dfrac{10}{100} = 0.1\text{ mm per year}$$.

**Compare loss with formation.** $$\dfrac{4\text{ mm per year}}{0.1\text{ mm per year}} = 40$$, so the loss rate is $$40\text{ times}$$ the natural formation rate at the fastest possible natural formation.

**Interpret the result.** Even under the most favourable natural soil-building conditions in the unit ($$100\text{ years}$$ per centimeter), erosion on steep highland farmland removes topsoil far faster than it forms, which is why the unit calls topsoil a precious, slow-forming resource and why conservation measures are indispensable.

questions.q:
A highland catchment of $$200\text{ hectares}$$ is losing topsoil by water erosion at the unit's mean rate for steep slopes of $$42\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$.
(a) Calculate the total annual soil loss from the catchment in tons.
(b) Given that this mean rate corresponds to an annual loss of approximately $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil, calculate the total volume of topsoil lost each year in cubic metres (take $$1\text{ m}^3$$ of topsoil $$= 1.3\text{ tons}$$), and express your answer to the nearest whole cubic metre.
(c) State one conservation measure from the unit that would directly reduce this loss on the sloping cultivated land, and one that would trap the sediment already being carried away.
questions.answer: (a) $$200 \times 42 = 8\,400\text{ tons per year}$$. (b) $$\dfrac{8\,400}{1.3} = 6\,461.5$$, so approximately $$6\,462\text{ m}^3$$ of topsoil per year. (c) Hillside terraces (or contour bunds) on the sloping cultivated land reduce detachment and runoff, while check dams built across active gullies trap the sediment and slow the water.
why: **Identify the mean loss rate and area.** The unit reports a mean soil loss of $$42\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$ on steep slopes, and the catchment area is $$200\text{ hectares}$$.
**Compute the total annual soil loss.** $$\text{Total loss} = 42\text{ tons/ha/year} \times 200\text{ ha} = 8\,400\text{ tons per year}$$.

**Convert tons of soil to volume.** Using $$1\text{ m}^3 = 1.3\text{ tons}$$, the volume is $$\dfrac{8\,400\text{ tons}}{1.3\text{ tons/m}^3} = 6\,461.5\text{ m}^3$$, which rounds to approximately $$6\,462\text{ m}^3$$ per year.

**Link the loss to the thinning topsoil layer.** The unit notes that the mean steep-slope loss represents an annual loss of about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil, roughly $$20\text{ times}$$ the possible soil replacement rate, so this volume represents a layer of fertile topsoil that natural formation cannot replace within a human lifetime.

**Select measures that reduce and trap the loss.** Hillside terraces are a physical measure that breaks slope length and traps water and sediment on sloping cultivated hills, and contour bunds intercept surface runoff and encourage infiltration on gently sloping croplands. Check dams are built across gullies to slow water velocity and trap sediment, preventing the gullies from widening.
